name: Olga Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Olga, thanks for fitting this in. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can give me your public line and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on a big new estate, two hundred houses, for one of the national housebuilders, out past the business park on Hollins Road. I'm with an agency, doing first fix, so that's studwork walls, floor joists, door linings, before the plasterers come in. Clock in at half seven, I usually get given a plot number and a drawing, and I work through it with whoever I'm paired with that week. I like it when a plot's finished and signed off, there's a little sticker, and I'm weirdly proud of my stickers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what's hard, or what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being slow when the pay's by the plot. The experienced lads get through two a week, I'm closer to one and a bit, so I earn less, and I left school early so I'm learning a lot of it on the job. My partner Tomas works nights in a parcel warehouse, so we barely see each other. We rent a flat in the new block by the station and we've got maybe three weeks of money if nothing goes wrong. I use one of the AI apps sometimes, mainly to double-check joist spacing or write emails to the agency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. So basically more of the same. I can do more of the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but it's handy for small stuff. That's what I'd tell the lads, and that's about what it is for me now. I don't really post online, maybe a comment in the agency group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I've got time to get faster without anything weird happening. My problem isn't robots, it's that I'm doing one and a bit plots a week instead of two. That's on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the estate and try to get onto a direct contract with the housebuilder instead of the agency, because then I get holiday pay. I'd aim to get up to two plots a week by summer. And I'd try to put a hundred a month aside, starting with dropping my phone contract to a cheaper one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's just normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being slow is on you. What would help you get faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, working with the same person for more than a week. They keep moving me around. When I was with Derek for a month, I nearly hit two plots, because he showed me his order of doing things. Then he went to another site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the estate work that worries you, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The housing market. If house sales slow down, the agency people go first, that's how it works. That happened two winters ago and I had five weeks with nothing. That's my real worry, not computers.

S0.say: It was overhyped, but it's handy for small stuff. That's what I'd tell the lads, and that's about what it is for me now.
S0.think: It means I've got time to get faster without anything weird happening. My problem isn't robots, it's doing one and a bit plots a week instead of two, and that's on me.
S0.do: Keeps working on the estate and pushes for a direct contract with the housebuilder for holiday pay. Aims to reach two plots a week by summer and save a hundred a month, starting with a cheaper phone contract.
S0.feel: Calm, as normal life carries on.
S0.quote: My problem isn't robots, it's that I'm doing one and a bit plots a week instead of two. That's on me.
S0.fieldNote: Olga measures herself in plots per week and takes responsibility for her speed. Her real fear is the housing market and agency workers being cut first, which already happened to her once. She is practical and numbers-minded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's sort of happening already, isn't it. The wall panels on half the plots come from a factory now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like anything, some people do well, some don't, and the trick is to be on the right side of it. I'd say the government should help people retrain, but I'm not going to stand outside with a sign about it. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, first fix is exactly the sort of thing that moves into factories. They already send whole wall panels with the studs in. If they send whole rooms, there's no first fix left on site, just someone bolting boxes together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see which way the housebuilder goes, maybe six months, and ask the site manager straight what they're planning. If the factory panels take over, I'd apply to the panel factory up the motorway, because that's where the jobs would be. I'd use the AI app more, maybe for learning to read the factory drawings, once a few others on site are doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A slow worry, the kind you have on the drive in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The panel factory's up the motorway. How would you get there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the problem, it's forty minutes and I don't drive. Tomas does, but he works nights. I'd have to learn to drive or move closer, and we've just signed another year on the flat. So it's not as simple as I made it sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about working in a factory instead of on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. It'd be dry and warm, and regular hours, which I'd honestly love. But it's a different kind of job, you're doing the same panel all day. I'd miss the sticker on the finished plot, if that makes sense.

S1.say: It's like anything: some people do well, some don't, and the trick is to be on the right side of it. The government should help people retrain, but I'm not going to stand outside with a sign.
S1.think: First fix is exactly the sort of thing that moves into factories. If they start sending whole rooms, there's no first fix left on site, just someone bolting boxes together.
S1.do: Waits about six months to see the housebuilder's direction and asks the site manager directly about plans. Applies to the panel factory if panels take over, and uses the AI app more for reading factory drawings once others on site do.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a slow worry on the drive in.
S1.quote: If they send whole rooms, there's no first fix left on site, just someone bolting boxes together.
S1.fieldNote: Olga sees the threat clearly because factory panels are already on her site. Her plan to follow the work to the factory is sensible but blocked by not driving and a new lease, which she admits once pressed. She'd miss the satisfaction of a finished plot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's not long at all. That's barely one lease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to do something now, not in a report. Pay people while they sort themselves out. I'm not usually one for that, I usually say get on with it, but two years is too fast for anyone to get on with anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think the agency drops me first, inside the first year. I'm slow, I'm agency, and there's hardly any other building work in town. Tomas's warehouse would go robot too, probably first, they're already testing it. So we'd both be out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start applying for anything with a contract straight away, the council, the hospital, cleaning even, whatever has a steady wage. I'd cut everything, no takeaways, cheapest phone, cancel the streaming. If it got bad, I'd ask my dad if we could move back in with him in Dunmore, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like being told the scaffold's coming down while you're still on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you hate moving back in with your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's fine, but he'd make it a lesson. You should've stayed at school, all that. And it's a two-bed with my brother still there. It'd be the sofa for me and Tomas. I'd do it, but I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, if you had to pick one thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car. Well, Tomas's car. It's eighty a month on finance and he only needs it because of the night shift. If he's not on nights, it goes. That's the first thing.

S2.say: The government needs to do something now, not in a report, and pay people while they sort themselves out. I usually say get on with it, but two years is too fast for anyone to get on with anything.
S2.think: The agency would drop me first, within the first year, because I'm slow and agency and there's hardly any other building work in town. Tomas's warehouse would go robotic too, so we'd both be out.
S2.do: Starts applying straight away for any contracted job with a steady wage, from the council and hospital to cleaning. Cuts all spending, starting with her partner's car finance, and asks to move back in with her father if things get bad.
S2.feel: Scared, as if the scaffold is coming down while she's still on it.
S2.quote: I usually say get on with it, but two years is too fast for anyone to get on with anything.
S2.fieldNote: Olga's usual self-reliant stance cracks in the fast picture, and she says so herself. She expects both her and her partner's jobs to go within a year. Moving back to her father's is a real, unwelcome fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's still quick but I could do something with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time if people start now, the government, the companies, and us. I'd say it like that, sensible, not angry. Everyone has a part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it gives me time to get off the agency, get a direct contract, and pick up a second skill before the end. I'd be thirty-two, still young enough to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get my driving licence, finally, and get on a direct contract. Then I'd look at what's still growing, maybe installing heat pumps or solar, the stuff the government's pushing, and do a course in that once a few people I know have done it. I'd save a hundred and fifty a month once Tomas and I sort the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way where I've got a list. I like a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the AI app now and then. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it more for studying, I think, like for the heat pump course. I'd ask it to explain the bits I don't get, because I'd feel stupid asking in class. That's what it's actually good for, the stupid questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't heat pumps be done by robots by 2031 too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Probably, at the end. But in the meantime there's years of installs in old houses, and old houses are awkward. I'd rather be awkward-house-ready than first-fix-on-a-new-estate-ready. That's the bit I'd bet on.

S3.say: There's time if people start now: the government, the companies and us. Everyone has a part, and I'd say it sensibly, not angrily.
S3.think: It gives me time to get off the agency, get a direct contract and pick up a second skill before the end. I'd be thirty-two, still young enough to start again.
S3.do: Gets her driving licence and a direct contract in the first year. Takes a course in heat pump or solar installation once people she knows have done it, using the AI app for study, and saves 150 a month once the car is sorted.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadied by having a list.
S3.quote: That's what it's actually good for, the stupid questions.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Olga plan step by step, and she bets on awkward old-house work outlasting new-estate first fix. She'd still wait for others to try a course first. She uses AI as a private tutor to avoid feeling stupid in class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's manageable if it's done properly, with proper retraining and nobody dumped. I'd say it like it's a normal thing to plan for, like pensions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine for most of it. Ten years of building, a second skill in the middle, and by the end, maybe I'm doing something else entirely. The end point still bothers me, I just can't see that far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the estate, get my plots up, get a direct contract, and wait a couple of years to see which new trades really take off before I pick one. I'd save a bit every month and build up maybe six months over the decade. I'd learn to drive, so I can follow work if I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my head, but mostly fine. I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the two-year picture you'd move back to your dad's. What's different here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Here I'd have time to make sure I never have to. That's honestly my main goal, not having to hear him say I told you so. Ten years is enough to make sure of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Tomas and you change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd maybe buy a flat in a few years instead of renting, if it looked okay. But I wouldn't do it until we'd seen a few years of how it's going. No point getting a mortgage if we're both out in 2034.

S4.say: It's manageable if it's done properly, with proper retraining and nobody dumped. It's a normal thing to plan for, like pensions.
S4.think: I'd be fine for most of it: ten years of building with a second skill in the middle, and maybe something else entirely by the end. The end point bothers me, I just can't see that far.
S4.do: Keeps working on the estate, improves her pace, gets a direct contract and waits a couple of years to see which trades take off before retraining. Saves monthly towards six months of cushion and learns to drive so she can follow work.
S4.feel: Mostly fine and sleeping well, with some unease at the back of her mind.
S4.quote: Here I'd have time to make sure I never have to.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years gives Olga room to wait for proof, which fits her steady style. Her main personal goal is never moving back to her father's. She'd hold off on buying a flat until the direction is clearer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Tomas and I would both be out in the same year with three weeks of money. What would help is a guaranteed wage for a while, maybe six months, while you find something, and help with driving lessons or travel, because the jobs won't be in this town.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about agency workers. We're always first out and nobody counts us properly. If you want to know who gets hurt first, look at the agency list on a building site.

headlineQuote: If you want to know who gets hurt first, look at the agency list on a building site.
portrait: Olga Khan is a 27-year-old agency first-fix carpenter on a 200-home estate, paid by the plot and still slower than the experienced crew. She rents near the station with her partner Tomas, who works nights in a parcel warehouse, and they hold about three weeks of savings. She's pragmatic and self-reliant, uses AI apps now and then, and waits for proof before changing. A stall leaves her calm, steady change makes her eye the panel factory, AGI by 2028 alarms her as both she and Tomas would lose work, and longer warnings let her plan a licence, a direct contract and a move into heat pump work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and Tomas would both be out of work in the same year with about three weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed wage for around six months while finding work, plus help with driving lessons or travel because jobs won't be in her town.
